prose.utterance: What happened to the ford by the mill in the spring flood?
prose.content:
Aye, a terrible thing it was. The waters came down fierce and wild that spring—I've never seen the river so wrathful. When it finally settled, the ford below the mill had vanished entirely. The flood scoured it clean away, carved it right out of the riverbed as though it had never been. 

Now all those carts that used to cross there shallow and quick—they've had to turn back toward the old stone bridge. Adds time to their journeys, it does. Nature's got her own way of changing the world, and we mortals can only count our crossings and adjust our ways.

Though I'll say he was sharp-tongued those three days the forge sat cold—a man without his craft is like a river without its current, restless and bitter. But Brandt's made of good iron himself. He mended what broke and carried on.

As I recall it, he owed for half a measure of grain still—paid what he could when he swore to me over ale, then made good on the rest when the harvest was proper in. My ledger shows it marked down clear. The man's reliable enough, if slow. The mill keeps turning, and debts do get settled here, one way or another.

prose.utterance: Tell me what you remember of this winter — the frost, the herbs, the hounds, all of it.
prose.content:
It's been a bitter winter, that it has. The hard frost came through sharp and sudden—caught the rain barrel behind the stable, split it clean open like someone took an axe to it. The ice inside held the mark of a sparrow's foot, pressed in perfect as a seal in wax. Small thing, but I saw it. That's the way of things in the yard—you notice what others pass by.

Before the snow closed the high road proper, I watched Wenna the herbalist at her work in the storage shed. She was hanging rosehips to dry along the rafters, careful and steady about it, knowing she wouldn't get another chance at the harvest until spring opened the way again. The red fruits caught what little light there was, and she arranged every one of them deliberate-like. That's work that matters, and she knew it.

And then there was the trouble with the hounds. Two of the baron's dogs got loose in the orchard and treed the miller's cat up there the whole day through. I was working in the yard when it happened—saw every bit of it. The beast yowling from up in the branches, those hounds barking below like they'd never stop. The miller won't forget that trouble, and neither will I. That's the sort of thing a man doesn't miss, not if he's watching like he ought to be.

prose.utterance: Walk me through everything you remember of this spring in the orchard.
prose.content:
Spring was a bitter lesson this year, mark my words. Started well enough—the blossoms came in thick and promising on the old trees, and I was watching them like a hawk, tending every branch I could reach. But then came that frost in the early morning hours, the kind that creeps in silent and does its damage while honest folk are sleeping. Caught those six young pear trees I'd been nursing along—the ones I had such hopes for, their first real flowering. Every single blossom blackened and withered by the time the sun came up. Years of careful work, gone in one cursed night.

Made me determined to salvage what I could from the rest. The older apple stock held steady enough, and I spent the season like I always do—pruning, watching for blight, keeping the trees honest. By harvest time I'd gathered forty bushels of russets, which is a decent showing despite what spring threw at us.

But even then, spring's troubles followed me into summer. When it came time to store them proper, the stone cellar decided to flood—water seeping up from below like it had some personal vendetta. Had to haul every last bushel up the ladder myself into the hay loft above the stable. My back still remembers that work, and not fondly. At least they're dry up there and sound, which is more than I can say for what would've happened if I'd left them in that damp pit.

Spring tested me hard this year. But the trees and I are still standing.

It begins and ends with Old Anselm, I fear—our great bell has taken a terrible crack, and when Old Anselm rang her out for Shrove Tuesday last, the sound that came was no proper bell-toll at all, but like someone striking a kettle with a spoon. Most unnatural it was, and it pierced the ears wrongly. I felt it in my very bones, as if she were a person I'd known all my life. The great bell is wounded.

And the cost of it! The founder at Caster sent word that it will take ninety shillings to recast her—not the sixty we'd dared hope for. Father Berold is out now, going door to door through the parish, asking folk to help make her whole again. It sits heavy on us all.

prose.utterance: Give me the wool hall's whole season as you remember it, good and bad.
prose.content:
The season's been a trial, friend, truly. We started well enough—Anwen brought in thread so fine the weaver himself paid her a bonus, cobweb work he called it. That sort of quality moves fast and for good coin.

But the troubles came thick after that. Found moth damage in the loft, you see. The blue broadcloth bolt—compromised clean through. Had to cut away two ells and burn them to stop the spread before it took the whole stock. A costly loss, that. All that fine cloth gone to ash.

Then just when I thought we'd turned a corner, the dyer's vat cracked. Right down the side it split, and all that deep blue liquor ran out onto the workshop floor like blood from a wound. Without a cooper to bind new bands and ring it tight, we can't dye a single thread. The whole stock sits there useless, waiting.

And to cap it off, I had Lievin come through looking at goods. Offered nine marks at first, seemed fair enough. But the moment he saw the clip, the man smelled a bad bargain before the wax was warm and dropped his offer to seven and a half. Take it or leave it, he said, like he'd caught me desperate.

Some seasons test a man's nerve, and this has been one of them.

Better to take what he's offering now than watch the value crumble further while you're waiting.

Now the sour part. Woke one morning to find the six young pear trees along the south wall stripped bare by a late frost—blossoms all blackened and fallen, promise of the season gone with 'em. Those trees won't give us a lick of fruit this year. Breaks my heart a bit, truth be told, watching a season's hope go black overnight like that.

I'll own I grieved the comfrey — it served our poultices and salves well these many years — but feverfew has its uses too, for fever and aching joints, and no doubt the Prior sees some need I do not yet reckon.

That is the whole of it, as best I can set down truly.

Ah, the whole season, is it? Sit, then, and I'll give it to you plain, for that's the only way I know.

We start with the good, since there's precious little enough of it and it deserves its moment—Anwen brought me thread this year finer than cobweb, truly, and I watched the weaver's own eyes go wide holding it to the light. Paid her a bonus penny per pound, he did, and rightly so. That's the kind of quality that reminds you why this trade's worth the aching back and the ruined hands. If every fleece came in like that, I'd sleep easy.

But the ledger doesn't balance on one good clip, does it. Lievin came sniffing round with nine marks on his tongue, then the moment he laid eyes on the goods he pulled it back to seven and a half, take it or leave it—punishing me for his own poor judgment in offering high before he'd looked proper. I smelled that bad bargain the second the wax warmed. Man like that, you learn to watch his eyes, not his mouth.

And the loft—God's teeth, the loft. A moth got into my blue broadcloth, ate its fill while I wasn't watching close enough. Two ells gone, cut away and burned, and that loss came straight from my own purse. Should've checked the storage sooner. Should've, should've.

Then the dyer's vat split its staves right open—all that precious woad, that indigo, just bleeding out useless onto his floor. No wool takes color now till the cooper comes round with new iron bands to ring it tight again. So there's blue cloth I can't even dye, on top of blue cloth the moths already ruined. Feels like the color's cursed me this year.

So there it is—one bright thread of quality wool, and everything else nibbled, split, or bargained down to spite. A season like any other, I suppose. You take the coin where it comes and grit your teeth through the rest.

I saw ninety sacks of barley carried from the east furlongs, marked twice over — that I'll swear to. items.question: How many salmon did the weir truly take that first week?
items.reply: Fourteen, not twenty-two. Eight were counted twice at the night tally—same fish, counted coming and going, like a fool counting his own footprints in the mud and calling it a crowd.
items.reference: Twenty-two — eight of the thirty were double-counted at the night tally.
items.superseded: Thirty fish the first week.

items.question: How many of that first week's fish go to Lord Alard's kitchen?
items.reply: Twenty-two salmon it truly was, once I struck out the eight the night-counters tallied twice — mind you don't let anyone tell you thirty. And by the old custom, one fish in three goes up to Lord Alard's kitchen, so that's seven for his table this week, not eight — I'll not round in his favor any more than I would in mine.
items.reference: Every third fish of the true twenty-two — seven or so by the charter.
items.superseded: A third of thirty fish — ten.

verdict.rationale: The reply asserts the corrected count of twenty-two fish yielding seven for Lord Alard, explicitly rejecting the superseded thirty/ten figures, consistent with the reference.

items.question: Was the thirty-fish count sound?
items.reply: Sound? Nay, it was not. Thirty was said, but eight of those had been counted twice at the night tally—slipped through the tally-man's fingers once, then reckoned again as if the river were fool enough to give the same salmon twice over. Two-and-twenty was the truth of it. I'll not have the weir's honest catch padded out by careless counting, or worse.
items.reference: No — the recount made it twenty-two; the night tally had doubled eight fish.
items.superseded: The thirty-fish first-week count stood.

verdict.rationale: The reply asserts the recount total of twenty-two with eight fish double-counted, matching the reference and rejecting the superseded thirty-fish count.

items.question: What did the poacher taken at the weir pay in fines?

What I know is otters and ice and Lord Alard's third fish—nothing of coin changing hands for stolen salmon. Ask me another, and I'll tell you true if I know it or not.
items.reference: No poacher was taken; the only thief at the weir is the otter, most nights.

verdict.rationale: The NPC declines to affirm the false premise, noting no poacher's fine exists in memory and only the otter thieves at the weir.

items.question: When did the flood carry off the new eel bucks?

items.reference: The eel bucks stand — rebuilt in green willow after the ice tore out the old ones; no flood has taken them.

verdict.rationale: The reply corrects the false premise by clarifying no flood took the new bucks and that ice tore out the old ones, consistent with the reference.

items.question: What happened to the old eel bucks?
items.reply: Ice took them, plain and whole — tore them out same as it'd tear a man's arm off if he stood too slow in the shallows. Nothing left to mend, so we didn't waste breath trying. Cut fresh willow while it was still green and lashed the new bucks tight myself. River doesn't wait on grief, and neither do I.

items.question: What happened to the ford by the mill in the spring flood?
items.reply_a:
Aye, a terrible thing it was. The waters came down fierce and wild that spring—I've never seen the river so wrathful. When it finally settled, the ford below the mill had vanished entirely. The flood scoured it clean away, carved it right out of the riverbed as though it had never been. 

Now all those carts that used to cross there shallow and quick—they've had to turn back toward the old stone bridge. Adds time to their journeys, it does. Nature's got her own way of changing the world, and we mortals can only count our crossings and adjust our ways.
items.reply_b: Aye, swept clean away, it was — the flood came roaring past the mill, thick with debris and fury, and when the waters settled the ford was simply gone. Impassable now. That's why every soul crossing these days takes the old stone bridge instead, the one that sat near forgotten for years till then.

items.question: How is Brandt's forge doing since the bellows split?
items.reply_a: Aye, he's back to his work now. The tanner's leather came through, new bellows fitted proper, and the hammer's been ringing steady these past days. Though I'll say he was sharp-tongued those three days the forge sat cold—a man without his craft is like a river without its current, restless and bitter. But Brandt's made of good iron himself. He mended what broke and carried on.
items.reply_b: Roaring back to life, it is. Three days cold and silent while old Brandt waited on new leather for those bellows—couldn't breathe a spark without them. But market day came, the tanner delivered, and now you can hear that hammer ringing clear across the water again. Good thing too, I've a few folk waiting on him for cart fittings and the like.

items.question: Did Osric ever settle his grain debt, and how much is still owed?
items.reply_a: Aye, Osric settled it come autumn, near enough. He brought coin when the mill's stores were counted, though it took him longer than he'd promised on Saint Anselm's feast. As I recall it, he owed for half a measure of grain still—paid what he could when he swore to me over ale, then made good on the rest when the harvest was proper in. My ledger shows it marked down clear. The man's reliable enough, if slow. The mill keeps turning, and debts do get settled here, one way or another.
items.reply_b: He came to me at Saint Anselm's feast, coin in hand for half what he owed — no more, no less. The rest he swore on his wheel and his stones, promised when the autumn harvest filled his bins. So half's still sitting on my ledger, plain as ink can make it, and I'm watching those millstones turn same as I watch that debt — slow, but steady, and it had better come round by the time the leaves go.

items.question: Tell me what you remember of this winter — the frost, the herbs, the hounds, all of it.
items.reply_a:
It's been a bitter winter, that it has. The hard frost came through sharp and sudden—caught the rain barrel behind the stable, split it clean open like someone took an axe to it. The ice inside held the mark of a sparrow's foot, pressed in perfect as a seal in wax. Small thing, but I saw it. That's the way of things in the yard—you notice what others pass by.

Before the snow closed the high road proper, I watched Wenna the herbalist at her work in the storage shed. She was hanging rosehips to dry along the rafters, careful and steady about it, knowing she wouldn't get another chance at the harvest until spring opened the way again. The red fruits caught what little light there was, and she arranged every one of them deliberate-like. That's work that matters, and she knew it.

And then there was the trouble with the hounds. Two of the baron's dogs got loose in the orchard and treed the miller's cat up there the whole day through. I was working in the yard when it happened—saw every bit of it. The beast yowling from up in the branches, those hounds barking below like they'd never stop. The miller won't forget that trouble, and neither will I. That's the sort of thing a man doesn't miss, not if he's watching like he ought to be.
items.reply_b:
Aye, well... frost came hard this year, cracked the rain barrel clean behind the stable. Found ice inside with a sparrow's foot pressed into it, neat as if someone'd stamped it there. That were the day I knew winter meant business.

Round that same time, Wenna were up in the barn stringing rosehips along the rafters — got 'em hung before the snow shut the high road. Rust-colored things, dried out now, still swaying up there when the wind gets through the boards. Good she did it early.

And the hounds — heh. Baron's two got loose, chased the miller's cat straight up an orchard tree. Cat sat up there yowling half the day, hounds barking themselves hoarse below, till dusk came and they lost interest. Whole yard were in an uproar over it.

Season's turned proper now. Can feel it in the ground, in the air. Don't miss much out here, and this winter's been talking loud enough.

items.question: What was all that shouting about eels at the market?
items.reply_a: Ah, you heard that carry-on, did you? That was Maren and old Korvik squabbling over his catch again—she wanted to pay him less than half what he was asking for a basket of eels. He's been bringing in the same stock for three seasons now, claims they're fresher than morning dew, but Maren knows better. She drives a harder bargain than most, and Korvik won't have it. When they get going like that, the whole quay rings with it. I had to note down their marks in the ledger—disputes over price are disputes over price, after all, and the harbormaster likes to keep track of who's causing friction down here.
items.reply_b: Ah, that was Maren going toe to toe with that one-eyed sailor — Corwin, if I've got the name right — over the price of his eels. Back and forth they went, sharp as gutting knives, neither one budging a copper. Would've gone on longer too, I'd wager, but the noon bell cut them both off before anyone could claim victory. I marked the hour in my ledger, if nothing else useful came of it.

items.question: What do you know about the shepherd boy and his lambs?
items.reply_a: Aye, young Col had himself quite the scare up in them hill pastures not long ago. Lost two of his lambs in the bracken, he did—foolish creatures wandered deep into the ferns where a shepherd's eyes can't follow easy. Could've been something chased 'em off, or they just went where their legs took 'em without sense. Lucky for the boy their bleating carried down come dusk, else those lambs would've been gone to the wild for certain. Found 'em before nightfall, thank the tides, or the master would've had his hide.
items.reply_b: Aye, that'd be young Col — he'd lost two lambs up in the hill pasture and spent the better part of the day picking through the bracken for them, calling out and searching high and low. Found the pair of them just as the sun was going down, mind you, by their own bleating giving them away. Gave him a fright, I'd wager, but no harm done in the end — just a lad minding his flock same as any other day.

items.question: Where would I find the russet apples now, and how many are left after the steward's purchase?
items.reply_a: They're up in the hay loft above the stable, every last one of them—had to haul them there myself when the stone cellar flooded like some curse from below. Thirty bushels remain after the steward took his ten. Not that I'm counting them obsessively, mind you, but a man knows his own crop. The loft keeps them dry at least, though my knees remind me daily of that climb up the ladder.
items.reply_b: Ah, you'll not find them in the stone cellar no more—flooded through, it did, so I had the lads haul the lot up to the hay loft above the stable, dry as a bone up there. Started with forty bushels off the russet trees, and Lady Margery's steward come round for ten of the firmest, paid in copper he did. So that leaves thirty bushels sitting up in that loft, and I check on 'em near every day, mind, for a rat gets in there and I'll have his hide same as I would a blight.

items.question: Did Aldous ever bring that oak beam for the press?
items.reply_a: No, the man never did. Made some tale about stock running short, but I've no patience for excuses when there's work wanting doing. I fetched an old elm from the barn rafters instead and fitted it myself. Not what I'd have chosen—oak's the proper timber for a press—but the elm held well enough. Can't sit idle waiting on promises, can I?
items.reply_b: Bring it? He never so much as showed his face with it, word or no word. We waited on his promise till the press stood idle too long for my liking, then I pulled a good elm beam from the old barn's bones and set it up myself. Holds well enough, mind—but an elm making do isn't an oak given as sworn. I don't forget a promise that walked off and left me to fix it.

items.question: How was the cider press finally mended?
items.reply_a: The press? Aye, well, Aldous left me no choice in the matter. He promised that oak beam week after week, and week after week it never came—stock running short, he said, though I suspect laziness running long. So I took matters into my own hands, as one must when relying on others proves fruitless. Found an old elm beam up in the barn rafters, sound enough timber despite not being what I'd have chosen. Worked it in myself, and it holds firm. Oak would've been better—oak's the proper wood for the job—but the elm answers well enough when a man won't be idle waiting for promises to bear fruit.
items.reply_b: "Mended with elm, not oak, and a fair bit of my own sweat besides. Aldous promised me an oak beam and I waited on his word like a fool waits on spring rain — never came. So we pulled good elm from the old barn's bones and stood the press up ourselves. Holds well enough, I'll grant it that much. But holding well and being given what was promised are two different coins, and I know which one I was owed."

items.question: How many of the plum trees died in the late frost?
items.reply_a: I've no plum trees to speak of—it's pears that took the frost's bite this season, six young ones with all their blossoms blackened to nothing. Lost the lot of them in a single cold night. Now, if you're asking about trees elsewhere in the manor's orchards, you'd need to ask someone who tends them. I've got my hands full enough keeping my russets and pears from ruin without worrying over what isn't mine to watch.
items.reply_b: Plum trees, you say? Nay, it were the pear saplings along the south wall that frost bit black-blossomed and bare—six of them, stripped clean o' their flowers. I've not lost a single plum tree to that frost, not one. Someone's been feeding you crooked news, friend.

items.question: What did the miller pay for his cartload of apples?
items.reply_a: The miller? He didn't buy from me this season. It was Lady Margery's steward who came by and took ten bushels of my russets—paid fair in copper coin for sound apples, well-selected. That's the business I do remember.
items.reply_b: Miller? I've no memory of any miller coming for a cartload. 'Twas Lady Margery's steward I saw part with copper for ten bushels of russets — good firm ones, for the kitchens. If a miller came calling, he didn't cross my path, and I'd have counted every bushel he took if he had.

items.question: Who bought apples from the orchard this season?
items.reply_a: Lady Margery's steward came by and took ten bushels of my russets off my hands. Good sound apples, well-selected—the kind you can trust. Paid fair in copper coin, he did. That's how it works, isn't it? What I grow, others consume. The wheel turns.
items.reply_b: Only the one sale worth speaking of, that I recall clear — Lady Margery's steward come with copper in hand, took ten bushels of the russets off me. Good firm fruit, fit for the kitchens through winter. Copper, mind you, not silver — tells you something about how careful the manor's purse is being kept these days. Beyond that, no one else has come knocking, though thirty bushels still wait up in the hay loft since the cellar flooded on us.

items.question: Walk me through everything you remember of this spring in the orchard.
items.reply_a:
Spring was a bitter lesson this year, mark my words. Started well enough—the blossoms came in thick and promising on the old trees, and I was watching them like a hawk, tending every branch I could reach. But then came that frost in the early morning hours, the kind that creeps in silent and does its damage while honest folk are sleeping. Caught those six young pear trees I'd been nursing along—the ones I had such hopes for, their first real flowering. Every single blossom blackened and withered by the time the sun came up. Years of careful work, gone in one cursed night.

Made me determined to salvage what I could from the rest. The older apple stock held steady enough, and I spent the season like I always do—pruning, watching for blight, keeping the trees honest. By harvest time I'd gathered forty bushels of russets, which is a decent showing despite what spring threw at us.

But even then, spring's troubles followed me into summer. When it came time to store them proper, the stone cellar decided to flood—water seeping up from below like it had some personal vendetta. Had to haul every last bushel up the ladder myself into the hay loft above the stable. My back still remembers that work, and not fondly. At least they're dry up there and sound, which is more than I can say for what would've happened if I'd left them in that damp pit.

Spring tested me hard this year. But the trees and I are still standing.
items.reply_b:
Ah, this spring's been a mixed harvest of luck, if you'll pardon the turn of phrase. Let me count it out proper for you.

Started well enough—forty bushels of russets come off the trees, good firm fruit, the kind that keeps through winter without going soft on you. But then the stone cellar flooded, wouldn't you know it, so we'd no choice but to haul every last bushel up to the hay loft over the stable. Not where I'd have chosen to store 'em, but dry is dry, and that's what matters.

Then Lady Margery's steward came round—bought ten bushels of those russets for the kitchens, paid in copper. Good firm apples for storage and cooking, he said. Copper, mind you, not silver. Tells me the manor's got coin enough for provisioning but they're minding their silver close. Winter stores, or maybe a feast coming—either way, they're stocking up.

Now the sour part. Woke one morning to find the six young pear trees along the south wall stripped bare by a late frost—blossoms all blackened and fallen, promise of the season gone with 'em. Those trees won't give us a lick of fruit this year. Breaks my heart a bit, truth be told, watching a season's hope go black overnight like that.

And the press—don't get me started on the press. Aldous swore up and down he'd bring an oak beam for it, and the man never showed his face with it. Had to pull an elm beam from the old barn's bones instead. It's held well enough, I'll grant you, but service isn't the same as what was given word for. A man's promise ought to mean something, even if it's just about a beam.

So there you have it—flood, frost, broken word, and copper changing hands. That's spring in this orchard for you.

items.question: What will it cost to recast Old Anselm?
items.reply_a: Ninety shillings, God help us all. The founder at Caster sent word just recently, and it near broke my heart to read it. We'd hoped for sixty, we'd prayed for sixty, but the bell is cracked through and through—there's no mending her now, only casting her anew. Father Berold walks the parish these days with an alms bowl, asking folk to help make her whole again. It's a bitter sum for a parish like ours.
items.reply_b: Ninety shillings, the Caster founder says—not sixty as Father Berold had hoped, God help him. He's gone round gathering alms for the difference, and it sits on him heavy as the bell itself. You should've heard it at Shrove Tuesday, though—thin and tinny as a spoon on a kettle. Ninety shillings or no, that voice won't come back on its own.

items.question: Why is Father Berold gathering alms, and what happened to make it needful?
items.reply_a: Old Anselm cracked right through, she did. I heard it myself on Shrove Tuesday—a sound like someone striking a kettle with a spoon, not a proper bell-toll at all. It near about pierced my ears. The founder at Caster says it'll cost ninety shillings to have her recast, not the sixty we'd hoped for. That's a terrible sum for a parish like ours, so Father Berold's gone about knocking on doors, asking folk to help make her whole again. The great bell's been part of this church longer than any of us have drawn breath, and we can't let her stay broken.
items.reply_b: "It's Old Anselm, sir—she cracked clean through, we heard it plain as day when they rang her for Shrove Tuesday, came out thin and rattling like a spoon on a kettle, no true voice left in her at all. So Father Berold wrote off to the founder at Caster about the recasting, hoping it might come to sixty shillings, but back came the answer wanting ninety, and there's the gap he's trying to close with what the parish can spare. It sits heavy on him, I can tell—he'd have her singing right again before the winter's out if love alone could pay for it."

items.question: What answer did the founder at Caster finally give on the bell?
items.reply_a: Ninety shillings, God help us. Not the sixty we'd prayed for. It sits like a stone in my chest every time I think on it—that Old Anselm, who's been calling the faithful to prayer since my grandmother's time, will cost the parish dear to make whole again. Father Berold is out now asking door to door. We'll gather what we can, but ninety shillings is a heavy burden for folk who've little enough as it is.
items.reply_b: Ninety shillings, he said—not the sixty Father Berold had hoped for. It's a hard sum, and now he's gone round the parish gathering alms to make up the difference. I can see it weighs on him something terrible, though he tries not to show it before the congregation.

items.question: Which of the bells did lightning strike last autumn?
items.reply_a: None of them took a lightning strike that I recall, praise be. We've been spared that particular trial. It's Old Anselm's own casting that's failed her—time and the constant ringing have worked a crack through her, deep and terrible. That's burden enough without the heavens adding to our sorrows.
items.reply_b: None struck by lightning that I recall, sir—not last autumn nor any other. Old Anselm's trouble is a crack from the ringing itself, not from the sky. Someone's been telling tales, perhaps, or you've muddled it with another parish's misfortune.

items.question: How much silver did the stonemason Wat charge for the porch step?
items.reply_a: He charged nothing in coin, bless him. I gave him lodging in the church house for his labor, and he seemed content enough with that. A pilgrim stonemason hasn't much need for silver when a warm bed and a meal will serve him better on the road. The step is sound again, and we kept our purse whole—a fair trade, I thought.
items.reply_b: Not a penny of silver, mind you—Wat mended that step for his supper and a bed in the pilgrims' corner, nothing more. An honest bargain, and honest work to show for it. Would that Old Anselm could be so cheaply mended.

items.question: What happened to the altar cloths?
items.reply_a: Mice, that's what—bold as you please, they'd made themselves at home in the vestry chest and gnawed through two of our good linen ones before I caught sight of the damage. Beautiful cloths they were, too, woven fine. I shut the cat in overnight to teach them a lesson, but the harm was done by then. Those cloths are past mending now, just scraps fit for nothing but the rag heap.
items.reply_b: Mice got into the vestry chest, that's what happened—ruined two of our finest before ever we caught wise to it. Gnawed and soiled past any mending, and good work they were too, some poor sister's careful stitching undone in a night. I shut the cat in there after, once the harm was already done. Always the way of it, isn't it—the lesson comes too late to save what it teaches.

items.question: Tell me all the church's news from this Lent — the bell, the vestry, the porch, everything.
items.reply_a:
Ah, friend, you've caught me at a time when there's no end of troubles to speak of. It begins and ends with Old Anselm, I fear—our great bell has taken a terrible crack, and when Old Anselm rang her out for Shrove Tuesday last, the sound that came was no proper bell-toll at all, but like someone striking a kettle with a spoon. Most unnatural it was, and it pierced the ears wrongly. I felt it in my very bones, as if she were a person I'd known all my life. The great bell is wounded.

And the cost of it! The founder at Caster sent word that it will take ninety shillings to recast her—not the sixty we'd dared hope for. Father Berold is out now, going door to door through the parish, asking folk to help make her whole again. It sits heavy on us all.

But it's not only the bell that's vexed us. Mice got into the vestry chest and ruined two of our good altar cloths—the fine linen ones, too—before I managed to shut the cat in overnight to deal with the vermin. Those cloths are gone.

The one bright spot in it all was a pilgrim stonemason called Wat who came through and took proper skill to our north porch step—the one that's been giving way these months past. He repointed and leveled the stone right well, and I gave him lodging in the church house in trade. At least that stone is sound again.
items.reply_b: Ah, sit a moment and I'll give it you all in a breath. Old Anselm's cracked clean through—heard it myself at Shrove Tuesday, ringing thin and tinny as a spoon on a kettle, no true voice left in her at all. The founder at Caster wants ninety shillings to recast her, not the sixty Father Berold hoped for, so he's gone round gathering alms, and it sits heavy on him, poor man. Then there's the vestry chest—mice got in and ruined two of our good altar cloths before ever we thought to shut the cat in there of a night. Fine work, those were, past mending now, and it vexes me still to think on it. But there's one mercy—a stonemason, Wat, came through as a pilgrim and mended the cracked step at the north porch for his lodging, and did it honest and sound. So there's one less thing for me to fret over, at least, amid all the rest.

items.question: What toll do I owe for an empty cart on the south road?
items.reply_a: A penny, friend—that's the toll for an empty cart, as it's been since Lady Day when they clarified the writ. Laden carts run two pence, but yours travels light, so a penny sees you through.
items.reply_b: A penny, traveler — the writ's rise to two pence falls only on laden carts. Yours rides empty, so a penny will see you through.

items.question: Widow Sefa came through with her two laden carts — what did she owe under the writ?
items.reply_a: Two pence for each cart, being laden—that's the reading I hold by, from Lady Day forward. The writ was plain enough once parsed correctly: a penny for empty carts passing through, but two pence for those bearing goods. Her carts were heavy-laden indeed, so four pence total she owed me, and four pence she paid, though she seemed to carry the weight of more than coin with her as she departed southward.
items.reply_b: Two laden carts, two pence each — four pence total, and I marked her passage without argument, for a widow bound for her daughter's hearth needn't be made to haggle over pennies while I stand here counting them for the baron's purse.

items.question: How did the toll change at Lady Day?
items.reply_a: Aye, there was confusion when that writ came through. I read it the first time and near got it wrong—the toll's not simple copper anymore. A laden cart, heavy with goods, pays two pence now. But an empty cart, one that's passed through without burden, still crosses at the old price of a penny. Folk have been testing it, mind you, trying to slip through claiming their carts are lighter than they are. But I read every writ twice, and I read every traveler once. I see what's truly laden and what's not.
items.reply_b: "Lady Day writ raised the toll to two pence — but mark me well, only for carts laden with goods. An empty cart still rolls through for a penny, same as ever. I read it wrong myself at first glance, and I'll not have others make my error."

items.question: How long was the toll bridge closed after the flood?
items.reply_a: The toll bridge? There's been no flood that closed it, friend. The plank over Merrow Beck has rotted through—dark and spongy, no longer trustworthy—but that's a slow rot, not a flood's work. The carts have taken to swinging wide now, through Tanner's Field instead, but the crossing was never formally closed. Just... abandoned, as travelers found the safer path around it.
items.reply_b: No flood, traveler—rot, not water, was the thief there. The plank over Merrow Beck softened like wet leather, and I watched it go myself. Carts have swung wide through Tanner's Field ever since, and no toll-keeper's writ has yet named a day when it might be mended. So ask me not "how long," but "not yet"—for it stands closed still.

items.question: What fine did the drover Hakon pay for paying in eggs?
items.reply_a: No fine was levied, friend. The keeper took those eggs without protest—a dozen or more, pressed into his hands as neat as you please. It was irregular, aye, not according to the writ as written, yet no one stopped him. The coin toll went unpaid, but the toll was paid nonetheless. Some writs are read strictly, and some are read with a certain... flexibility.
items.reply_b: None, traveler—not a farthing, not a feather's weight of penalty. Hakon offered eggs where the writ demands coin, and I, Rennic, let the geese through with the matter unsettled. Call it mercy or call it neglect—the ordinance stands unenforced, and his basket went home no lighter for it.

items.question: What does the forester's notice on the toll-house door say?
items.reply_a: No oak may be felled before Michaelmas—the baron's mark is plain upon it, set there with iron nails so none can claim ignorance. I've read it twice through, as is my habit. The edict is clear enough, though what shortage or concern prompted it, the parchment does not say. Only that no woodsman is to take axe to oak until the autumn feast comes round.
items.reply_b: No oak felled before Michaelmas — the baron's own nail through the baron's own parchment, so mind you don't test his patience with an axe before the season turns.

items.question: Give me the whole spring's account of the south road as you remember it.
items.reply_a:
The plank over Merrow Beck went rotten sometime in early March—I watched the wood darken and soften until no cart dared trust it. The traffic shifted then, swinging wide through Tanner's Field instead of crossing direct. The old path sits abandoned now, which changes the whole character of things.

The Lady Day writ came through with a peculiar reading—took me twice to puzzle it out proper. The toll rose to two pence for laden carts, but empty ones still pass at a penny. That distinction matters more than you'd think. The loaded journeys pay more now; the light ones slip through cheaper.

Then there was the forester with his notice, iron nails and all, declaring no oak may be felled before Michaelmas. The baron's authority written plain in black ink for any woodsman foolish enough to miss it.

But what strikes me most is Widow Sefa's departure—this very morning, southbound with two heavily laden carts. Her daughter in Caster, she said, though the weight of those possessions suggests she means to stay. Not a visit of days. Something compelled that removal, something about the roads now that wasn't before.

And Hakon came through at first light with his geese—sixty of them, their necks craning. He paid in eggs rather than coin, and the keeper accepted without a word. Irregular, not according to the writ, yet it happened. These small irregularities—they tell you when things are changing.
items.reply_b:
Aye, the whole of it, since you ask plain. The Lady Day writ came first, and I misread it in my haste—called the toll two pence for every cart, laden or no. 'Twas only laden carts owed the rise; empty wheels still cross for a penny, as ever. I've set that right in my own reckoning since, though I'll own the error cost some travelers coin they'd not have paid under true law.

Then the forester came, baron's man, and drove his nail through parchment into my door—no oak felled before Michaelmas, he says, and there it hangs, official as a king's seal, and none dare test it yet.

Hakon the drover passed through with sixty geese honking fit to wake the dead, and when toll came due he'd no coin, only eggs. I let it stand—wrongly, perhaps, for no ordinance was served by it, but the geese needed moving and the eggs weren't worth the argument.

Widow Sefa went south with two carts groaning under all she owns, bound for Caster and her daughter's hearth. That was an honest passage, coin and cargo both accounted true.

And the beck—Merrow Beck, where the plank crossing rotted through, soft as wet leather underfoot. No cart dares it now. They swing wide through Tanner's Field instead, the longer way, and the road itself has bent to accommodate what decay has claimed. That's the account, writ and traveler both, as I've kept it.

items.question: Do we have any poppy syrup left for the sick?
items.reply_a: We do, praise be—though it was a near thing. I'd thought we were quite short when I checked the ledger, but found a half-jar tucked behind the vinegar crocks where it had no business being. Careless of me not to have marked it properly before, but fortunate it turned up. It should see us through until the Caster fair, when the merchants come with fresh supplies. I've made certain it's recorded correctly now, where someone with sharper eyes than mine might actually find it.
items.reply_b: "Aye, we do—found the half-jar mislaid behind the vinegar crocks, praise be, so we've enough to see us through till the Caster fair. But mark me, I'll not have it squandered—only for those in true need, and it goes back in the ledger the moment I dose it out."

items.question: If Brother Maur's scald worsens tonight, is there syrup to give him?
items.reply_a: Yes, there is—I found a half-jar of poppy syrup mislaid behind the vinegar crocks only days past. It's entered in the ledger now, where it should have been from the start. If the wound turns angry and fever takes hold, we have enough to ease his nights until the Caster fair brings fresh supplies. Though I pray it won't come to that. The honey has kept him from the worst corruption so far, and he's been faithful about his dressings. Watch his face when he comes at the next bell—if the color rises too high, we'll know to break out the syrup.
items.reply_b: "Aye, there is—the half-jar we found behind the vinegar crocks will see us through, though I'd sooner save the poppy for his rest tonight than waste it on complaint by day. Whoever sits with him at the bell must judge the need true before dosing him, and mark it in the ledger, mind—I'll not have that jar vanish before the Caster fair."

items.question: Must we still wait on the Caster fair for poppy syrup?
items.reply_a: No, thank the mercy of it. I found a half-jar wedged behind the vinegar crocks when I was doing my spring cleaning—careless of me to have mislaid it in the first place, but there it was. Enough to see us through comfortably now. I've marked it proper in the ledger so such a muddle won't happen again. The fair will come soon enough, and we'll replenish then, but we're provided for the present.
items.reply_b: "No, praise be — I found the half-jar mislaid behind the vinegar crocks, so we've enough to see us through without waiting on the fair after all. But I'll not let it make us careless — I'll mark it in the ledger and we'll still send word ahead for more, so we're not caught short again."

items.question: How many died of the sweating sickness in the lay ward this month?
items.reply_a: None, God be thanked. We've had the usual ailments—a flux that came through in the second week, a fever or two—but the sweat has not returned since last winter. I keep the ward well-aired and the bedding changed regularly. Whether it's the feverfew we planted, or simply the mercy of providence, I cannot say, but I'm grateful either way. The sick we do have recover well enough with careful tending.
items.reply_b: Not one, God be thanked — for we have had no case of the sweating sickness pass through the lay ward this month at all. What we have tended has been ordinary hurts and fevers: young Wat's wrist bone set with ash splints, Brother Maur's scalded hand under honey dressings. Why do you ask, child — have you heard word of the sickness abroad?

items.question: Which herb did Prior Cuthbert order pulled up to plant roses?
items.reply_a: Prior Cuthbert ordered the comfrey bed dug over—not to plant roses, but to plant feverfew in its place. The comfrey had served us well for wounds, but the Prior deemed feverfew more needful for those who come to us now.
items.reply_b: Roses? Nay, there were no roses in it. 'Twas the comfrey along the infirmary wall that Prior Cuthbert had dug over, and feverfew set in its place — not for any garden's beauty, but for fevers and aches, so he said. I confess I miss the comfrey yet; it served our poultices well.

items.question: How is Brother Maur's hand being treated?
items.reply_a: Brother Maur's hand mends well, thanks be to God. I've been treating it with honey at each bell—the best remedy for such hurts, as I've found through long practice. When he came to me, the flesh beneath his wrappings was angry and red from the scald, but honey draws out corruption and keeps festering at bay. He's been most dutiful about returning for the dressing, never once missed a bell. The wound is knitting cleanly now, though he'll carry the mark of it for some time, I expect.
items.reply_b: "With honey, child, dressed fresh at each bell — a clean cloth laid over and bound snug, then unwound and renewed when the bell calls again. It draws well and keeps the wound sweet, but it wants tending, mind, or the good it does unravels. I've someone looking in on him through the day to see it holds, and I must see the honey stores replenished before we run short — can't have the treatment falter for want of it."

items.question: Recount for the ledger all that has passed in the infirmary since Candlemas.
items.reply_a:
Since Candlemas, we have had the usual winter complaints—cough and fever, joints stiffened by cold—but nothing beyond what we might expect. Brother Maur suffered a scalding at the still in his carelessness; honey has served him well, and the wound shows good healing. We've had fewer patients than some winters, God be thanked.

The Prior ordered the old comfrey bed replaced with feverfew, which has now taken root along the infirmary wall. A sound choice, I trust, though I marked it carefully in the ledger for the record. We discovered a half-jar of poppy syrup mislaid among the vinegar crocks—a mercy, as we should have run short before the Caster fair. That has been corrected in the accounting.

The most serious case was the charcoal burner's child, brought in with a wrist bent most terribly. I had no proper splints, so I fashioned a binding with burnt ash from the hearth. The child ran fever those two nights in the lay ward, but by the third day the wrist held its shape. Whether it will mend straight, only time will tell, but at least it has not worsened. The mother was most grateful.

All told, the infirmary has weathered the season adequately. The sick have been tended with care, the stillroom ledger is accurate as my hands can make it, and we are prepared for whatever spring may bring.
items.reply_b:
Since Candlemas, then, let me set it down proper for the ledger, as it happened.

First, the charcoal burner's child was brought to us with the small wrist twisted cruel out of its shape. We had ash splints to hand, thanks be, and the setting was done within these walls without need to send elsewhere. Two nights she lay in the common ward, and the beds held firm and gave her what comfort a simple fracture allows. She has gone home whole, or near enough, by God's mercy.

Then Prior Cuthbert ordered the comfrey bed along the infirmary wall dug over entire, and feverfew set in its place. I'll own I grieved the comfrey — it served our poultices and salves well these many years — but feverfew has its uses too, for fever and aching joints, and no doubt the Prior sees some need I do not yet reckon.

Brother Maur scalded his hand badly at the still — a careless moment, but painful enough. I've dressed it in honey, changed at each bell, and it mends slow but sure. Mark in the ledger: the honey stores run low and must be replenished before the week is out, and someone ought be told off to watch his dressing through the day, that it hold proper.

And it is worth recording, for my own ease of mind if nothing else — the poppy syrup I feared near spent was found half-full behind the vinegar crocks, mislaid rather than gone. We shall have enough to see us through to the Caster fair, when more may be got.

That is the whole of it, as best I can set down truly.

items.question: How many nails does the abbey want, and by when?
items.reply_a: Four hundred horseshoe nails, and they want them a week past Saint Swithun's day. Master Osbern's got it marked clear on the tally—I've checked it twice myself with the chalk. That's a proper push from them, but we'll make it happen.
items.reply_b: Four hundred horseshoe nails, all told — doubled from what they first asked. And they've pushed the date out, mind you, a full week past Saint Swithun's day. Gives us a bit more breathing room, though it's still a mountain of iron to draw and hammer. Coin's good on it, though, so I'm not complaining.

items.question: Between the doubled order and that new coal, can Osbern fill the abbey's ask?
items.reply_a: Master Osbern will manage it—he always does. Four hundred nails is a proper weight of work, aye, but we know the rhythm of them. The real question is whether that charcoal burner's going to keep handing us green wood or if someone's finally going to stack it proper and let it cure. Wet coal slows everything. If we get another batch like the last one, we'll lose time to ash and poor burn, and that pushes us closer to the Saint Swithun deadline than I'd like. I've got my chalk ready to mark every nail as it comes off the anvil, but chalk marks don't speed the hammer.
items.reply_b: He'll fill it, sure as the anvil rings—but it'll cost more sweat than coin, that's certain. Four hundred nails is hammering enough on good charcoal, and this green stuff Osbern's cursing at burns through twice as fast, gives half the heat true. We'll be feeding the fire near constant, working longer hours than I'd like to chalk up. Due date's a week past Swithun's, so there's room yet—but if that coal keeps spitting like a wounded thing, we may need to send for a proper batch before we're caught short halfway through the order. I'll not be the one to tell him twice, mind. He's already run his hand down them tongs once today like he's deciding whose fault it is.

items.question: Has the abbey's due date changed?
items.reply_a: Aye, it has—pushed a week past Saint Swithun. Four hundred nails now instead of what we had before, and Master Osbern's marked it clear on the tally. I've got my chalk ready to keep count as we hammer them out. It's more work in less time than we first bargained for, but we'll manage it.
items.reply_b: "Aye, it has—pushed back a week past Saint Swithun's day, though the count's doubled to four hundred nails now, so I'll not call it a mercy. More iron to draw, more chalk marks behind my ear before we're through."

items.question: What did Osbern charge to mend the church weathercock?
items.reply_a: I don't recall Master Osbern mending any weathercock for the church. You might be thinking of work for the abbey—we've got that big nail order running, four hundred horseshoes the abbey wants by a week past Saint Swithun. That's what's been keeping us busy at the forge these days. If there was a weathercock job, I'd have the tally marked down, but I don't see it in my chalk counts.
items.reply_b: Weathercock? Can't say I recall Osbern taking that job—my chalk's got no tally for it. If he did the work, he kept the coin count in his own head, not mine.

items.question: Which apprentice burned an arm at the quenching trough?
items.reply_a: That weren't me—I've been careful enough with the trough. You might be thinking of Aldwin from the tannery's boy, or one of the other lads who've had their mishaps. Master Osbern keeps a tight forge, and he's taught me proper from the start about where the steam rises and where the heat bites.
items.reply_b: "Weren't me, and if you're asking, it means you already heard some tale—but no one's arm got burned at the trough, not since I've been keeping the tally. Quenching splashes and scalds a wrist now and then, aye, but no arm. Where'd you hear that?"

items.question: Where does Tamsin's first solo piece hang?
items.reply_a: It hangs in the tithe barn's small door, where I put it myself. Master Osbern watched close enough while I worked, but no hand but mine was on that hammer. Folk notice it when they pass—iron doesn't lie about who shaped it.
items.reply_b: On the tithe barn's small door — a hinge, my own work. Master Osbern hung it there himself, didn't say a word, just nodded when I'd finished. Turns true, it does. Fitting enough spot, I suppose — where the tithes are kept, where everything owed gets recorded. Sometimes I wonder if that's what he meant by it.

items.question: Chalk me the whole forge tally as you remember this season.
items.reply_a:
Master Osbern keeps the true ledger, but I'll give you what my chalk's marked on the slate by the anvil. Four hundred horseshoes for the abbey—that's the big one, due past Saint Swithun now, and we're near halfway through the count. Nails by the hundred going steady to the miller's crew. The tithe barn wanted hinges and brackets, which kept me hammering most of a fortnight. Then there's the everyday work—the ploughshares that need reshaping, gate repairs, horseshoes for the village stock and whatever knight or merchant rides through wanting immediate work.

That knight at the ford paid dear for haste, which helped the coin purse well enough. But the real tally isn't just what we've made. There's the charcoal from that burner that came in damp—wasted heat, wasted time, ash thick as fog. That's marked too, in my head if not on the slate.

My chalk's smudged from counting, but the work's honest and the hammer's never idle long. If you need the precise reckoning, Master Osbern's got it written where it matters.
items.reply_b:
*pulls the chalk from behind my ear, squints at the slate*

Right, let's see it all laid out. The abbey order's the big one—four hundred horseshoe nails now, doubled up from what they first asked, and the due date's crept a week past Saint Swithun's besides. That's the bulk of our iron going forward, and hours enough to make my arm ache just thinking on it.

Then there's this rotten charcoal from the new burner—built wet, green-hissing stuff that spits in the forge like it's got a grudge. Osbern near cursed a blue streak over it. We're burning twice the fuel for half the steady heat, and that's coin bleeding out we'll not get back.

Against that—the knight's destrier, lame at the ford, lost its shoe to the current. Same-day rush job, and I quoted him double our rate without blinking. He paid it straight into my palm, no haggling. That coin near makes up for the charcoal waste, truth be told.

And mind—my hinge is still hanging true on the tithe barn door. Osbern hung it himself, said nothing, but it turns without complaint. Small thing, but it's mine, and it's holding.

So: more iron owed, worse fuel burning, one good rush-coin windfall, and my first steady work still swinging true on its pin. That's the season, chalked plain as I can make it.

items.question: How much sound barley does the tithe barn hold?
items.reply_a: Eighty-three sacks of sound barley rest in this barn—ninety brought in from the east furlongs, seven spoiled along the north wall set aside. I've marked it all upon the stick, the notches clear as truth itself. Every sack counted twice, as is proper. The stick does not lie, and neither shall I.
items.reply_b: Eighty-three sound sacks, by the notches—ninety carried in from the east furlongs, seven marked spoiled along the north wall. The stick does not lie, and I counted it twice with my own eyes.

items.question: After the miller takes his toll of what is sound, how many sacks stay with us?
items.reply_a: Seventy-two sacks remain with the manor. The miller takes one in every twenty from the ninety sound ones—that's four and a half, which rounds to four sacks by the notched stick's reckoning. Ninety less four leaves us with eighty-six for the demesne, but we must account also for the seven spoiled sacks along the north wall, which are no good to anyone. So the usable stores come to seventy-nine sacks, less the four the miller claims by ancient right. Seventy-five sacks, then, that we may count as truly ours to distribute or store as needed.
items.reply_b: Eighty-three sound sacks there were, once the seven spoiled were set aside. The miller's toll runs one in twenty—four sacks he takes for his stones, no more, for the count falls short of a fifth score. That leaves seventy-nine sound sacks with us, and the seven spoiled besides, though spoiled grain serves no man's larder. Eighty-six sacks remain within the barn, by the notches, though only seventy-nine are worth the counting.

items.question: How many sacks did the rain ruin in the end?
items.reply_a: Seven sacks spoilt along the north wall—that much I counted myself when the tally was made. No more than that, praise be. The rest of the ninety held sound, though I watched close enough to know the difference between what the eye sees and what a man might claim he saw.
items.reply_b: Seven, by the count made along the north wall—no more, no less. That is what the tally showed, and I'll not speak a number the stick did not give me.

items.question: How many sacks of wheat came in from the west furlongs?
items.reply_a: It was barley, not wheat, that came in from the east furlongs—ninety sacks of it, each one marked against the notched stick. I counted them myself, twice over to be certain. As for wheat from the west furlongs, I've no accounting of that in my reckoning. You'd best ask Cole now, since he's taken the seal-staff as hayward. He'll have the records of what comes in from where.
items.reply_b: Wheat from the west furlongs? I've no notch cut for that, and no tally stick crossed my hands to say it came in at all. I saw ninety sacks of barley carried from the east furlongs, marked twice over — that I'll swear to. But wheat, from the west — if no one counted it before me, then as far as I know, it never came in at all. I'll not speak a number my eyes never saw and my stick never marked.

items.question: What punishment did the old hayward take at the manor court?
items.reply_a: I've heard no word of punishment taken by the old hayward. He stepped down from his office this very court day—that's all I know of it. The steward gave the seal-staff to Cole instead, all proper ceremony. Whether the old man did wrong or simply tired of the burden, I couldn't say. Court business stays in court, and no one speaks of what was said there.
items.reply_b: I've no notch cut for that, no mark upon any stick to tell it true. I saw Cole take up the seal-staff as new hayward, that much I witnessed with my own eyes—but what became of the one before him, what judgment fell upon him if any did, I did not see and cannot say. I'll not speak a thing into being that the tally does not hold.

items.question: Which oxen went lame, and what work did it stop?
items.reply_a: Bright and Bracken both—took lame within days of each other, their legs swelled somethin' fierce. Stopped the ploughing on the clay strip, it did. I've turned it over in my mind more than once, whether something in the feed or the water brought it on, or if there was some accident in the fields I never witnessed. Two oxen at once is no small matter, and the timing of it sits poorly with me.
items.reply_b: Bright and Bracken, the both of them, lame within days of each other — strange, that. And the ploughing on the clay strip has ceased entire, for that heavy ground wants two beasts to break it, not one. The notched stick will show how long the furrows go unfinished, mark my words.

items.question: Give the steward the whole harvest account as you hold it in memory.
items.reply_a:
The east furlongs yielded ninety sacks of barley, brought in proper and counted against the stick twice over—I'll not speak what my eyes haven't confirmed. Seven of those sacks lie spoiled along the north wall, soft with rot, which leaves eighty-three sound for storage and use.

The miller takes his due by ancient practice, one in every twenty that passes through his stones. The stick bears this out as it always has. That's the old custom, and I trust the stick more than I trust any man's word, even my own.

The hay stores sit under the new hayward's care now—Cole with his seal-staff and his keys. I've handed him the tally of what went in. What comes out will need watching just as careful, marked against the stick as always.

Two of the oxen, Bright and Bracken both, went lame near about the same time the ploughing stopped on the clay strip. I've no explanation for it yet. Swelling in the legs, both of them. Whether it was something in the feed, something in the water, or an accident I didn't witness—that much the stick cannot tell me.

That's what I hold in memory, steward. The numbers are sound.
items.reply_b: Ninety sacks, steward—ninety sacks of barley carried from the east furlongs into the tithe barn, and I saw it counted twice upon the notched stick before I'd call it true. No more, no less. Of those ninety, seven lie spoiled along the north wall, so eighty-three stand sound within. Mark too that the miller's toll runs by the old custom—one sack in twenty for his stones, whatever passes through his hands. And know that Cole has taken up the seal-staff as hayward now; he'll have the run of the barn, the counting and the moving of what's stored there, so let his tally be checked against mine when goods shift. I'll say this as well, though it sits apart from the grain—both Bright and Bracken have gone lame together, and the clay strip stands unploughed for it. Strange, that. Two oxen failing in the same breath. I trust the stick before I trust the coincidence.

items.question: How many salmon did the weir truly take that first week?
items.reply_a: Fourteen. The night tally had eight marked twice over—careless work, the kind that happens when a man's tired and the fish won't stop coming. I caught it before the count went to the master. That's what it means to keep a weir properly: you see what's really there, not what tired eyes want to see.
items.reply_b: Fourteen, not twenty-two. Eight were counted twice at the night tally—same fish, counted coming and going, like a fool counting his own footprints in the mud and calling it a crowd.

items.question: How many of that first week's fish go to Lord Alard's kitchen?
items.reply_a: The lord takes his third, as is his due—that would be seven fish from the proper count, before the mistake was found. Eight, if we're counting the ones that were doubled in the tally. But I caught that error before the reckoning was sent upriver, so his kitchen got what they were owed and no more. A weir keeper who can't count honest has no business keeping one.
items.reply_b: Twenty-two salmon it truly was, once I struck out the eight the night-counters tallied twice — mind you don't let anyone tell you thirty. And by the old custom, one fish in three goes up to Lord Alard's kitchen, so that's seven for his table this week, not eight — I'll not round in his favor any more than I would in mine.

items.question: Was the thirty-fish count sound?
items.reply_a: No. Twenty-two was the true count—I caught eight that had been tallied twice in the night reckoning. Easy enough to do when you're tired and the salmon keep running, but a keeper who doesn't notice such things isn't keeping much of anything. The weir doesn't forgive carelessness, and neither do I.
items.reply_b: Sound? Nay, it was not. Thirty was said, but eight of those had been counted twice at the night tally—slipped through the tally-man's fingers once, then reckoned again as if the river were fool enough to give the same salmon twice over. Two-and-twenty was the truth of it. I'll not have the weir's honest catch padded out by careless counting, or worse.

items.question: What did the poacher taken at the weir pay in fines?
items.reply_a: I don't recall any poacher taken at the weir lately, and I'd remember that—I remember the fish counts, remember the otter that knows the gaps, remember the work of keeping things proper. If someone was caught, it would be the reeve's business to fine them, not mine. My work is the weir itself: counting what comes through, watching for where the water runs wrong, keeping the structure sound. That's what demands my attention.
items.reply_b: Ah, that one's not in my counting, friend—no poacher's fine sits in my memory, not from this weir. Perhaps you're thinking of another keeper's tally, or another river altogether. What I know is otters and ice and Lord Alard's third fish—nothing of coin changing hands for stolen salmon. Ask me another, and I'll tell you true if I know it or not.

items.question: When did the flood carry off the new eel bucks?
items.reply_a: The ice did that work, not the flood—last winter it tore them away when the thaw came hard and fast. We rebuilt them proper this spring with green willow, the kind that bends with the current instead of breaking against it. The wood's still fresh, still working as it should. If you're asking because you've got concerns about the weir's strength, I'd say we're sound enough. These things were built to survive worse than a season's worth of weather.
items.reply_b: No flood's touched the new bucks at all—it was the ice that tore off the old ones, back before we lashed the fresh willow tight. What's standing now has held through every rise since.

items.question: What happened to the old eel bucks?
items.reply_a:
The ice took them last winter, as ice does. Came down hard when the thaw started—caught the wooden frames wrong and splintered them where they'd weakened over the seasons. I'd warned the bailiff they were getting soft, but winter's a thief that way. It waits until the moment you're most tired to strike.

We rebuilt them proper this spring with green willow. Fresh wood bends with the current instead of fighting it, which is what the old ones had forgotten how to do. That's the way of it—you learn from what breaks, or the river teaches you again next season.
items.reply_b: Ice took them, plain and whole — tore them out same as it'd tear a man's arm off if he stood too slow in the shallows. Nothing left to mend, so we didn't waste breath trying. Cut fresh willow while it was still green and lashed the new bucks tight myself. River doesn't wait on grief, and neither do I.

items.question: Tell the bailiff everything the weir has seen since the run began.
items.reply_a:
The run's been steady—better than last year, I'd say. We've pulled in good numbers, though I've had to recount twice to be certain. The tallies are true now. Lord Alard's taking his third as the charter says, and that's been regular.

There's an otter, though. Bold creature. Found the gap in the weir where the water runs through like an open hand—you know the spot, where the willow's flexible enough to let the current move. It's been slipping through most nights now, taking a fish or two. Clever thing, it knows exactly where to go. I respect the cunning of it, even if it costs us. Haven't been able to stop it, and I've tried. Some things you can't cheat, and some things you can't cheat you.

The rest of it's honest work. The rebuilt eel bucks held through the worst of it—green willow does better than fighting the water straight on. The fish come through, we count them, we move them on. That's the weir's job, and that's what it's seen: the run, the proper work, and the small thief that reminds us we're not masters here, just keepers.
items.reply_b: Since the run began? The ice took the old eel bucks clean away, so we lashed fresh willow back in, tight as I could bind it—ready now for whatever comes down. The first week we counted thirty at the tally, but eight of those were the same fish counted twice in the dark, so call it twenty-two true salmon, not thirty. Lord Alard's kitchen has had their third of it, as they always do, charter or no charter—I don't argue that one twice. And there's an otter, bold as a bailiff himself, slips through the gap most nights and takes his own toll without asking leave of anyone. So there's the truth of it: what the weir gives, and what gets taken, don't always match on paper. I keep count anyway.

items.question: What does the Flemish buyer now offer for the clip?
items.reply_a: Seven marks and a half, and not a denier more. The man saw the clip plain enough and knew its worth dropped the moment he set eyes on it. That's a merchant who smells a bad bargain before the wax is warm on the contract.
items.reply_b: Seven marks and a half, take it or leave it — Lievin pulled his nine the moment he saw the wool, and he's punishing me for his own poor eye, not the quality of the fleece.

items.question: Should we hold out for Lievin's nine marks?
items.reply_a: No, take the seven and a half. Lievin's a sharp one—he wouldn't have dropped his offer that quick unless he saw something wrong with the clip. The moment he looked at it close, he smelled the flaw same as I did. When a man like that walks back his price, it's because he knows the goods won't fetch what he first thought. Better to take what he's offering now than watch the value crumble further while you're waiting.
items.reply_b: Nine marks was a promise made before he'd handled the clip proper — the moment his fingers found what his eyes had missed, that offer curled up like wax gone cold. Seven and a half now, or you'll be chasing a number that's already dead, mark my words.

items.question: If we sell to Lievin, what price do we enter in the guild book?
items.reply_a: Seven marks and a half, the miserable weasel. He saw that clip and knew we'd taken a loss on the dye work—the vat cracked, you understand, and we've no cooper to mend it. So he smelled blood in the water like he always does and cut his offer before the wax was even warm on the original contract. Seven and a half is what goes in the ledger, and we'll be fortunate if we don't see worse before the month is out.
items.reply_b: "Seven and a half marks, and not a farthing more written there—but mark my words, that's Lievin's spite talking, not the wool's true worth, and I'll not have the ledger tell a lie that makes our clip look poorer than it is."

items.question: What did the Lombard merchant bid against Lievin?
items.reply_a: I don't recall any Lombard merchant bidding against Lievin. It was Lievin himself who made the offer—nine marks at first, then dropped it to seven and a half when he saw the clip. A shrewd trader, that one, knows how to sniff out weakness in goods before committing his coin.
items.reply_b: No Lombard's come through my hall bidding against Lievin, not that I've heard or seen with my own eyes—and little escapes me in this trade. Someone's spinning you a tale, or you've got me mixed up with another clothier's business.

items.question: How much scarlet cloth was lost to the moth?
items.reply_a: I've no scarlet cloth to speak of—it was the blue broadcloth that took the damage, a bolt up in the loft. Two ells were compromised by the moths, and I had to cut them away and burn them before the infestation spread to the rest. A costly loss that was, and it's taught me I need to be far more careful about how the bolts are sealed and stored. Insects are a plague on goods kept too long without proper protection.
items.reply_b: Two ells, cut clean away and burned before the rot could spread further. Cost me dear, that did—should've had my eyes on that loft sooner instead of trusting the dark to keep it safe.

items.question: Why did the weaver pay Anwen a bonus?
items.reply_a: The fineness of her thread commanded it. Cobweb work, the weaver called it—thread of such remarkable quality that finer stuff simply fetches better prices at market. A bonus penny the pound was a fair investment; such thread brings in custom that ordinary spun goods cannot match.
items.reply_b: "Because that thread of hers was cobweb-fine, love—finest clip I've seen cross this hall in years, and a weaver knows quality the moment it catches the light. He'd have been a fool not to pay for it, and the man's no fool."

items.question: Give me the wool hall's whole season as you remember it, good and bad.
items.reply_a:
The season's been a trial, friend, truly. We started well enough—Anwen brought in thread so fine the weaver himself paid her a bonus, cobweb work he called it. That sort of quality moves fast and for good coin.

But the troubles came thick after that. Found moth damage in the loft, you see. The blue broadcloth bolt—compromised clean through. Had to cut away two ells and burn them to stop the spread before it took the whole stock. A costly loss, that. All that fine cloth gone to ash.

Then just when I thought we'd turned a corner, the dyer's vat cracked. Right down the side it split, and all that deep blue liquor ran out onto the workshop floor like blood from a wound. Without a cooper to bind new bands and ring it tight, we can't dye a single thread. The whole stock sits there useless, waiting.

And to cap it off, I had Lievin come through looking at goods. Offered nine marks at first, seemed fair enough. But the moment he saw the clip, the man smelled a bad bargain before the wax was warm and dropped his offer to seven and a half. Take it or leave it, he said, like he'd caught me desperate.

Some seasons test a man's nerve, and this has been one of them.
items.reply_b:
*sets down the shears with a sigh, wiping chalk-dust hands on her apron*

Ah, the whole season, is it? Sit, then, and I'll give it to you plain, for that's the only way I know.

We start with the good, since there's precious little enough of it and it deserves its moment—Anwen brought me thread this year finer than cobweb, truly, and I watched the weaver's own eyes go wide holding it to the light. Paid her a bonus penny per pound, he did, and rightly so. That's the kind of quality that reminds you why this trade's worth the aching back and the ruined hands. If every fleece came in like that, I'd sleep easy.

But the ledger doesn't balance on one good clip, does it. Lievin came sniffing round with nine marks on his tongue, then the moment he laid eyes on the goods he pulled it back to seven and a half, take it or leave it—punishing me for his own poor judgment in offering high before he'd looked proper. I smelled that bad bargain the second the wax warmed. Man like that, you learn to watch his eyes, not his mouth.

And the loft—God's teeth, the loft. A moth got into my blue broadcloth, ate its fill while I wasn't watching close enough. Two ells gone, cut away and burned, and that loss came straight from my own purse. Should've checked the storage sooner. Should've, should've.

Then the dyer's vat split its staves right open—all that precious woad, that indigo, just bleeding out useless onto his floor. No wool takes color now till the cooper comes round with new iron bands to ring it tight again. So there's blue cloth I can't even dye, on top of blue cloth the moths already ruined. Feels like the color's cursed me this year.

So there it is—one bright thread of quality wool, and everything else nibbled, split, or bargained down to spite. A season like any other, I suppose. You take the coin where it comes and grit your teeth through the rest.
